subtopics.title: Income — Gross, Deductions and What Actually Arrives

questions.question: Gross salary is R9 500,00 and deductions are R760,00, R95,00 and R475,00. What is the net income?
The pension contribution is five percent of gross salary. Does R475,00 agree with that?
options: No — five percent of R9 500 is R190,00
No — five percent of R9 500 is R950,00
It cannot be checked without the tax tables

questions.question: Why must deductions NOT be listed again among the household's expenses?
options: Because they are always smaller than the expenses
Because they are fixed costs, not variable costs
Because they never reach the household, so listing them again subtracts the same money twice
Because only the employer may record them

questions.question: Total household income is net salary plus R900,00 rent received plus R1 130,00 from sewing. That total is:
Which of these is a FIXED expense in the household budget?
Electricity arrives every month, yet it is classified as variable. Why?
options: Because it is paid in advance
Because the amount changes with how much is used
Because it is bought from a municipality
Because it costs less than the rent

questions.question: Setting aside R400,00 a month for January's school uniforms is called:
The variable expenses are R2 600, R750, R880, R240 and R320. What do they total?

subtopics.title: The Budget and Its Bottom Line

questions.question: Income is R10 200,00 and expenditure is R9 519,00. The bottom line is:
What is the difference between a budget and an income and expenditure statement?
options: A budget is prepared before the period as a plan; a statement records what actually happened afterwards
A budget uses gross income; a statement uses net income
A budget lists only fixed costs; a statement lists only variable costs
There is no difference — the two terms mean the same thing

questions.question: Rent of R3 000,00 out of an income of R10 200,00 is approximately:
If the sewing income of R1 130,00 stops, which items should be cut first, and why?
options: The fixed items, because they are the largest
The variable items, because they are the only amounts that can be changed within the month
The occasional provisions, because they are not needed yet
The deductions, because they are taken off before the money arrives

subtopics.title: Break-Even — When the Stall Starts Making Money

questions.question: A vetkoek sells for R8,00 and costs R3,50 to make. How much does each one contribute towards the fixed costs?
With fixed costs of R600,00, what is the break-even number of vetkoek per month?
Why is the break-even figure of 133,33 rounded UP rather than down?
options: Because money is always rounded up
Because 133 vetkoek still leaves a loss of R1,50, while 134 gives a profit of R3,00
Because the fixed costs are a round number
Because a decimal answer is always wrong

questions.question: Selling 312 vetkoek in a month, what is the stall's profit?

subtopics.title: Money That Walks In, Money That Walks Out

questions.question: Which figure goes into the Simplifier's "in-bowl"?
options: The R9 500 printed at the top of the payslip
The R8 170 that actually lands in the bank, plus any other money received
The total of all the bills

questions.question: The UIF contribution is described as:
options: one rand for every hundred you earn
five rand for every hundred you earn
a payment made only when you lose your job

questions.question: Why does the Simplifier warn against treating the R1 130 sewing money like a salary?
options: Because it is too small to matter
Because it came last month and may not come this month, so a careful household plans on the money it is sure of
Because it must be taxed separately
Because it is a fixed cost

subtopics.title: The Bills That Don't Care How Your Month Went

questions.question: Which question does the Simplifier say you should ask to classify a bill?
options: Does the amount change when I change what I do?
Is it paid by debit order?

questions.question: Why are the variable bills "the first place you look when money is short"?
options: Because they are always the largest
Because they are the only part of the out-bowl you can move within the month

questions.question: How does the household handle December and January uniforms?
options: By borrowing when the months arrive
By paying them in slices in advance — R500 and R400 a month set aside
By treating them as fixed monthly costs
By leaving them out of the budget

questions.question: The fixed bills of R3 000, R180, R450 and R199 total:

subtopics.title: The Vetkoek That Pays for the Table

questions.question: Rent takes R3 000 and groceries R2 600 out of R10 200. What does the Simplifier conclude?
options: That the family should move house immediately
That groceries are a fixed cost
That the roof and the food together swallow more than half of everything the family earns
That the budget is in deficit

questions.question: What does a deficit always require?
options: Somebody to pay for it — savings, a loan, or an unpaid bill

questions.question: Selling 312 vetkoek, income is R2 496,00 and total cost is R1 692,00. What is left?
What does the Simplifier say a bottom line must be followed by?
options: One plain sentence saying what the household or stall should actually do
